name: Everest & Solukhumbu
tagline: Sherpa valleys, sacred peaks and the Everest trail
meta_description: Everest & Solukhumbu: Sherpa villages, Tengboche, Gokyo lakes, Everest Base Camp, Solu's monasteries, seasons, permits, Lukla flights and altitude advice.
summary: Solukhumbu is the Sherpa homeland of north-east Nepal and the district that holds Everest. High Khumbu, inside Sagarmatha National Park, has Namche, Tengboche, Gokyo and Base Camp; lower Solu has forested hills, apple orchards and old monasteries. Go in October–November or March–May, with time to acclimatise.
intro: Solukhumbu runs from the green, terraced hills of Solu in the south to the ice of Everest, Lhotse and Cho Oyu on the Tibetan border. Sherpas call the two halves Shorong and Khumbu. Most visitors know only Khumbu, the high valleys above Lukla, where the Everest trail climbs from pine forest to yak pasture to glacier over about a week.

Khumbu is a living Sherpa homeland, not a wilderness. Villages such as Namche, Khumjung, Thame and Pangboche have been farmed and herded for centuries; gompas such as Tengboche and Pangboche hold the valley's spiritual life; and mountains such as Khumbila are homes of protector deities. Since 1976 the area has been Sagarmatha National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979.

Solu, below, is gentler and much quieter: Phaplu's airstrip and Salleri's bazaar, the cliff-top Chiwong Gompa, Junbesi and its great nunnery of Thubten Chholing, Ringmo's apple orchards and the rhododendron forests of the Lamjura La. It was the old walking route to Everest before Lukla's airstrip opened in 1964, and it still makes the best slow approach.

We plan this region around altitude. Above Namche, at about 3,440 m, the body needs time, and the safe pattern is slow climbing, rest days and a willingness to turn back. Within that frame there is a lot to choose from: Base Camp and Kala Patthar, the Gokyo lakes, the high passes, or a week of Sherpa villages and monasteries that never goes above 4,000 m.

story.title: The people of the east and their hidden valley
paras: Sherpa means 'people of the east', from shar, east, and pa, people. The Sherpas' ancestors came from Kham in eastern Tibet, crossing the Nangpa La glacier pass west of Thame roughly 500 years ago and settling in Khumbu and Solu. They brought Tibetan Buddhism of the Nyingma school, a language close to Tibetan, and a clan system whose members still marry outside their own clan. For centuries they farmed barley and buckwheat, herded yaks and traded salt and grain across the Nangpa La.

Potatoes, which reached Khumbu in the 19th century, changed the economy, feeding larger villages at high altitude. Monasteries followed: Pangboche, attributed to Lama Sangwa Dorje and considered the oldest; Thame; Tengboche, founded in 1916 with the blessing of Tibet's Rongbuk Monastery; and in Solu, Chiwong around 1920 and Thubten Chholing in 1968, built by lamas who fled Tibet after 1959.

The 20th century brought the climbers. Sherpas walked to Darjeeling to carry loads for British expeditions on the Tibetan side of Everest in the 1920s and 1930s. When Nepal opened to foreigners after 1950, the approach moved to Khumbu, and on 29 May 1953 Tenzing Norgay, who grew up in Thame, and Edmund Hillary reached the summit. Hillary returned again and again; his Himalayan Trust built Khumjung's school in 1961, the Lukla airstrip in 1964 and Kunde's hospital in 1966.

Today trekking and climbing are the economy of Khumbu, with lodges in every village and Sherpa companies running expeditions. The changes bring hard questions: crowding on Everest, rubbish, the risks borne by climbing Sherpas, and a warming climate that grows glacial lakes, as the flood that struck Thame in August 2024 showed. Sherpa families are meeting them with the same mix of faith and practicality that built the valleys.

legend: Sherpa tradition holds that Khumbu is a beyul, a hidden valley blessed by Guru Rinpoche, the eighth-century teacher Padmasambhava, as a sanctuary to be opened in times of trouble. Its guardian is Khumbu Yul Lha, the god of the Khumbu country, who lives on the sacred peak of Khumbila above Khumjung and is shown riding a white horse. Everest itself is home to the goddess Miyolangsangma, and climbers ask her permission at a base camp puja before setting foot on the mountain.
people: Sherpas are the main community of high Khumbu and many Solu villages, speaking Sherpa, a Tibetic language, and practising Nyingma Buddhism. Lower Solu is mixed: Rai, Magar, Tamang, Newar and Khas families farm the terraces and trade in Salleri. Rai and Tamang men and women from lower valleys work as porters across the region. Nepali is the shared language; English is common in lodges.

untold.fact: Sagarmatha National Park was created in 1976 and inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979. It covers about 1,148 square kilometres of Khumbu, including Everest, Lhotse, Cho Oyu and the Sherpa villages.
untold.source: UNESCO World Heritage listing: Sagarmatha National Park

untold.fact: The name Sherpa comes from shar, east, and pa, people. Sherpa ancestors migrated from Kham in eastern Tibet roughly 500 years ago, crossing the Nangpa La into Khumbu.
The Gokyo and associated lakes in upper Khumbu were designated a Ramsar wetland of international importance in 2007, covering about 7,770 hectares.

untold.fact: Edmund Hillary's Himalayan Trust built Khumjung School in 1961, the Lukla airstrip in 1964 and Kunde Hospital in 1966, all at the request of Sherpa communities.
untold.source: Wikipedia: Edmund Hillary; Wikipedia: Kunde Hospital

untold.fact: Thame, a small village west of Namche, is the home of Kami Rita Sherpa, who holds the record for the most ascents of Everest, and of Apa Sherpa, who held it before him.

taste.name: Solja (Sherpa butter tea)
taste.text: Solja is black tea churned with salt and butter, the drink of every Sherpa kitchen from Junbesi to Gorak Shep. Hosts refill your cup the moment it drops. It tastes more like a thin soup than tea, and on a frozen morning above 4,000 m it makes complete sense.

highlights.title: Namche and its Saturday market
highlights.text: Khumbu's trading town at about 3,440 m, where every trek rests two nights. On Saturday mornings porters who walked for days from Solu and the Rai hills sell rice, vegetables and eggs on the terraces, keeping an old trade alive.

highlights.title: Tengboche and Mani Rimdu
highlights.text: The largest gompa in Khumbu, founded in 1916 and rebuilt after the 1934 earthquake and the 1989 fire, faces Ama Dablam from a forested saddle. In October or November its courtyard fills for the masked dances of Mani Rimdu.

highlights.title: Kala Patthar and Base Camp
highlights.text: From Gorak Shep, walk onto the Khumbu glacier to Everest Base Camp at about 5,364 m, then climb Kala Patthar, about 5,644 m, for the trek's great view of Everest's summit above the Khumbu Icefall.

highlights.title: Gokyo lakes and Gokyo Ri
highlights.text: A chain of turquoise lakes beside the Ngozumpa glacier, listed as a Ramsar wetland in 2007. Gokyo Ri above shows four 8,000 m peaks at once: Cho Oyu, Everest, Lhotse and Makalu.

highlights.title: Khumjung, Thame and the Sherpa story
highlights.text: Hillary's first school of 1961 and a revered yeti scalp in Khumjung; Tenzing Norgay's childhood village and the old salt road to Tibet in Thame. These villages tell how Sherpa life and Everest climbing shaped each other.

highlights.title: Solu's monasteries and orchards
highlights.text: Below Khumbu, Chiwong Gompa on its cliff above Phaplu, Junbesi's great nunnery of Thubten Chholing, Ringmo's apple orchards and the rhododendron forests of the Lamjura La make a gentle, low-altitude week.

getting_there: Almost everyone reaches Khumbu by air. Small aircraft fly from Kathmandu to Tenzing-Hillary Airport at Lukla, about 2,860 m, in about 35 minutes. Since 2019, in the peak months, roughly March to May and October to November, most Lukla flights have operated from Ramechhap airport at Manthali, a 4–5 hour pre-dawn drive from Kathmandu, with a 20-minute flight from there. Flights run only in clear weather, so keep spare days. There is no road to Lukla or Namche. Solu is reached by jeep from Kathmandu to Salleri and Phaplu in 10–12 hours via Okhaldhunga, or by a short flight to Phaplu when services run. From Phaplu, the old walking route reaches the main Everest trail below Lukla in 4–5 days. Check current status before you travel, as flight routings change each season.
permits: Trekkers in Khumbu need two permits: the Khumbu Pasanglhamu Rural Municipality entry permit, about NPR 2,000 per person, collected at Lukla or on the trail just beyond, and the Sagarmatha National Park entry permit, about NPR 3,000 for foreigners, paid at Monjo. Since April 2023 Nepal requires foreign trekkers in national parks and conservation areas to trek with a licensed guide; in Khumbu, where the local municipality runs its own permit, the rule has been applied unevenly. Climbing peaks such as Island Peak needs a separate climbing permit. Solu outside the park needs no trekking permit. Check current status before you travel.

months.weather: Namche about −10 to 6 °C; dry, clear, very cold nights
months.summary: January is the coldest month and the quietest. Skies are often clear and crisp, with fine mountain views, but nights in Namche drop well below freezing and higher lodges above Dingboche may be closed. Lower routes work well: Namche, Khumjung and Tengboche, or the Solu villages around Phaplu and Junbesi. Lukla flights run on clear mornings with fewer passengers. Carry a sleeping bag rated to about minus 20 °C.
months.tip: Stay below about 4,000 m and pack for nights of minus 10 °C or colder.

months.weather: Namche about −8 to 8 °C; mostly dry, some snow
months.summary: February stays cold but days lengthen. Sherpa families celebrate Gyalpo Lhosar, the Tibetan new year, with gompa visits, new prayer flags and house-to-house calls, usually in February or early March. Trails are quiet and villages hospitable. Snow can fall on the high routes, and some high lodges remain closed. Good for a cultural week around Namche, Khumjung and Tengboche rather than a high trek.
months.tip: Carry a white khata and small gifts if you hope to visit families at Lhosar.

months.weather: Namche about −4 to 12 °C; warming, clear mornings
months.summary: March opens the spring season. Days warm, high lodges reopen and rhododendrons begin to flower in Solu and the lower Dudh Koshi forests. Mornings are clear, with more cloud and haze in the afternoons. Nights above 4,000 m are still very cold. A good month for Base Camp, Gokyo and the Lamjura La forests near Junbesi. Lhosar sometimes falls in early March.
months.tip: Start walking early to enjoy clear views before afternoon cloud builds.

months.weather: Namche about 0 to 15 °C; mild days, afternoon cloud
months.summary: April is peak spring trekking. Rhododendron forests below Tengboche and around Junbesi are in full flower, days are mild and trails busy. Expedition teams set up Everest Base Camp, which becomes a tent city below the Khumbu Icefall. Expect haze and afternoon cloud, and occasional snow higher up. Lukla flights may operate from Ramechhap. Book lodges and flights early.
months.tip: Book Lukla flights and good lodges well ahead; April is as busy as October.

months.weather: Namche about 4 to 17 °C; warmer, hazier, pre-monsoon showers
months.summary: May is the Everest climbing season's climax, with summit pushes in the middle of the month and a busy Base Camp. Days are warm, but haze and afternoon showers increase as the monsoon approaches, and views are less reliable. Thame's Mani Rimdu usually falls in May. Chhukung and Island Peak are busy with climbers. Plan to be off the trail by early June.
months.tip: Walk in the mornings; afternoons in May often bring cloud and showers.

months.weather: Namche about 8 to 18 °C; monsoon begins, frequent rain
months.summary: The monsoon arrives in June. Lukla flights are often cancelled, trails below Namche are muddy and leech-prone, and cloud hides the peaks for days. Higher up, rain falls as snow and the valleys turn green. Sherpa villages hold Dumji, honouring Guru Rinpoche's birth, around June or July. Only for experienced repeat visitors with flexible plans.
months.tip: Allow several spare days for flights if you visit in the monsoon.

months.weather: Namche about 9 to 18 °C; heavy monsoon rain, cloud
months.summary: July is the heart of the monsoon. Rain is frequent, flights unreliable, landslides close Solu's roads and leeches fill the lower forests. High pastures are green and full of flowers and herders, and Dumji may be celebrated in some villages. Few lodges are busy. We do not recommend trekking now except for those who know the region well and accept delays.
months.tip: Carry rain gear, leech socks and patience; plans will change.

months.weather: Namche about 8 to 17 °C; monsoon rain, some breaks
months.summary: August remains wet, with clouded peaks and frequent flight cancellations, though breaks in the rain become a little more common late in the month. Hindu pilgrims visit the Gokyo lakes and Dudh Kunda below Numbur at the Janai Purnima full moon. High flowers are at their best. Roads in Solu are often blocked. Most travellers should wait for autumn.
months.tip: If you must go, choose short routes with easy retreat and check flight status daily.

months.weather: Namche about 4 to 15 °C; monsoon easing, clearing late
months.summary: September is a transition. Early in the month rain and cloud linger; by the end, skies clear and the autumn season begins. Trails are green and quiet, and Solu's apples ripen around Phaplu and Ringmo. Lukla flights become more reliable as the month goes on. A good time for those who want quieter trails and do not mind some cloud.
months.tip: Plan late-September departures for the best balance of clearing skies and quiet trails.

months.weather: Namche about −2 to 13 °C; dry, clear, stable
months.summary: October is the classic month: clear skies, stable weather, sharp mountain views and comfortable daytime temperatures. Trails and lodges are at their busiest, and Lukla flights may operate from Ramechhap. Tengboche's Mani Rimdu often falls in October or November. Base Camp, Gokyo and the high passes are all in good condition. Book everything early.
months.tip: Book flights and lodges months ahead, and start each day early for the clearest views.

months.weather: Namche about −5 to 10 °C; dry, very clear, colder nights
months.summary: November brings the clearest air of the year and slightly fewer trekkers than October. Nights grow colder, well below freezing above Dingboche, but days are bright and still. Mani Rimdu at Tengboche may fall in early November. Chiwong in Solu also stages its own festival in autumn or early winter. An excellent month for Base Camp, Gokyo, Chhukung and photography.
months.tip: Pack a sleeping bag rated to about minus 20 °C for Lobuche and Gorak Shep.

months.weather: Namche about −8 to 7 °C; dry, clear, cold
months.summary: December is cold, dry and quiet. Views are often excellent and trails nearly empty, but nights are bitter above 4,000 m and some high lodges close towards the end of the month. Shorter routes to Namche, Khumjung, Tengboche and Pangboche are pleasant, and Solu is mild by day. Lukla flights are usually reliable in clear weather.
months.tip: Check which high lodges are open before planning a Base Camp trek in late December.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit the Everest region?
faqs.a: October and November are the best months, with clear skies, stable weather and good views. March to May is the second season, with rhododendrons and warmer days but more haze. December to February are cold but clear and quiet. June to September is monsoon, with cloud, rain and frequent Lukla flight cancellations.

faqs.q: How do I get to the Everest region from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Fly to Lukla, about 35 minutes from Kathmandu, or in peak seasons drive 4–5 hours to Ramechhap airport at Manthali and fly 20 minutes from there. There is no road to Lukla. For Solu, drive 10–12 hours to Phaplu or fly when services run. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do I need a guide to trek in the Everest region?
faqs.a: Since April 2023 Nepal requires foreign trekkers in national parks and conservation areas to trek with a licensed guide. In Khumbu, where the local municipality runs its own permit, the rule has been applied unevenly. A licensed guide also helps with altitude, lodges and flight delays. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What permits do I need for Everest and Khumbu?
faqs.a: The Khumbu Pasanglhamu Rural Municipality permit, about NPR 2,000, and the Sagarmatha National Park entry permit, about NPR 3,000 for foreigners. Climbing peaks such as Island Peak needs a separate climbing permit. Solu outside the park needs no trekking permit. Fees change; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I avoid altitude sickness on the Everest trek?
faqs.a: Climb slowly: above 3,000 m, raise your sleeping altitude by no more than about 500 m a night and take a rest day every 1,000 m or so, usually in Namche and Dingboche. Drink 3–4 litres a day, avoid alcohol and tell your guide about symptoms early. If they worsen, descend.

Sherpas are an ethnic community whose ancestors came from Kham in eastern Tibet roughly 500 years ago. The name means 'people of the east'. They speak Sherpa, practise Nyingma Buddhism and live in Khumbu and Solu. Many work as mountaineering and trekking guides, but Sherpa is an ethnicity, not a job title.

faqs.q: Can I visit the Everest region without trekking high?
faqs.a: Yes. A 6–8 day trip from Lukla to Namche, Khumjung and Tengboche reaches about 3,900 m and gives views of Everest from Syangboche and Tengboche. Solu offers monasteries, villages and orchards between 2,000 and 3,000 m around Phaplu and Junbesi. A helicopter flight is another option.

faqs.q: How much does an Everest Base Camp trek cost?
faqs.a: A 14-night teahouse trek with a licensed guide, porter, permits, Lukla flights and lodges costs from about USD 1,450 to 1,900 per person, twin sharing. Gokyo treks cost similar amounts. Better lodges and helicopter returns cost more. Budget extra for drinks, showers, charging, Wi-Fi and tips.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Solu and Khumbu?
faqs.a: Solukhumbu District has two parts. Khumbu, the high north, lies mostly inside Sagarmatha National Park and holds Namche, Tengboche, Gokyo and Everest. Solu, the lower south, around Phaplu, Salleri and Junbesi, is greener, warmer and quieter, with forests, orchards and old monasteries. Sherpas call Solu Shorong.
